Means
meenz
n. (that by which an end is accomplished; instrument, method; chiefly in the KJV in the phrases by no means and by all means)
From Old French meien, from Latin medianus, middle — a means is what stands in the middle between an intention and its accomplishment. The KJV's commonest use is adverbial, in the emphatic negatives and positives.

Biblical Definition

Means is the middle term between a purpose and its end, and Scripture handles it in two ways that must be held together. First, in the emphatic negative, it marks what God will not do: he keeps mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, “and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:7). That clause stands inside the great self-revelation of God's name, immediately after the mercy, and the two are not in competition — they meet at the cross, where the guilty are cleared precisely because guilt was not waived but borne. Our Lord uses the same emphatic form of the believer's safety: “nothing shall by any means hurt you” (Luke 10:19), and Paul of the last things: “Let no man deceive you by any means” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). Second, and positively, means describes the instruments God appoints for his ends. Paul's missionary rule is the classic case: “I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). This is the doctrine of means in a sentence. God has decreed the salvation of his elect, and he has decreed the preaching, the travel, the flexibility, and the self-denial by which they will be saved. Election never makes the means unnecessary; it is precisely what guarantees they will not be wasted.

Webster 1828 Definition

That by which an end is accomplished. God will by no means clear the guilty, and Paul will by all means save some — the appointed instruments through which God's decree reaches its end.

expand to see more

MEANS, n. plu. [from mean, middle.] That which is used to effect an object; instrument; that which is subservient to an end.

2. Income; revenue; resources; as, a man of means.

3. By all means, without fail; certainly; at all events.

4. By no means, not at all; certainly not; not in any degree.

5. By any means, possibly; at all; as, if by any means I might attain, Phil. 3.

Key Scripture

Exodus 34:7 — "Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation."

1 Corinthians 9:22 — "To the weak became I as weak, that I might gain the weak: I am made all things to all men, that I might by all means save some."

2 Thessalonians 2:3 — "Let no man deceive you by any means: for that day shall not come, except there come a falling away first, and that man of sin be revealed, the son of perdition;"

Luke 10:19 — "Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy: and nothing shall by any means hurt you."

Modern Corruption

The doctrine of election is set against the use of means, so that God's decree is treated as making evangelism, prayer, and diligence unnecessary — the old fatalist error Scripture never permits.

expand to see more

The charge that Reformed theology kills missions is as old as the theology, and it survives because the objection is easy to state and the answer requires two thoughts at once. God has chosen a people; God has also appointed how they will be gathered. The decree includes the means, and it is a confusion to imagine a decreed end floating free of the road to it. Paul is the proof, since no writer states election more strongly and none travelled further. In 1 Corinthians 9 he makes himself servant to all, becomes as a Jew to Jews and as weak to the weak, and explains it by that I might by all means save some. In Acts 18 the Lord tells him at Corinth I have much people in this city — and the effect of that assurance is not that Paul leaves but that he stays a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.

The principle to recover is the balance inside God's own name. Exodus 34 declares him merciful, gracious, longsuffering, forgiving iniquity — and in the same breath says he will by no means clear the guilty. Any doctrine of grace that quietly drops the second clause has stopped describing the God of Scripture. Penal substitution is what holds them together: the guilty are not cleared by a waiver but by a substitute, so that God is just and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus (Romans 3:26).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The KJV's by no means renders emphatic Hebrew and Greek constructions of double negation; by all means renders pantos, altogether, in 1 Corinthians 9:22.

expand to see more

Hebrew infinitive absolute construction — the doubled verb of Exodus 34:7 rendered by no means clear.

Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be clean, to acquit; the verb God says he will not do for the guilty.

Greek pantos (G3843) — altogether, by all means; Paul's missionary purpose in 1 Corinthians 9:22.

Greek ou me (G3364) — the emphatic double negative, rendered by no means and in no wise.

Greek tropos (G5158) — a manner or way; by any means in 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

Usage

"Of what God will not do: that will by no means clear the guilty (Exodus 34:7)."

"Of appointed instruments in mission: that I might by all means save some (1 Corinthians 9:22)."

"Of guarding against deception: let no man deceive you by any means (2 Thessalonians 2:3)."
